question: Y162
answer:
REGULATORY AFFAIRS MEMORANDUM — Outside time limits for FDA action on a De Novo request accepted without an additional-information submission; 21 CFR Part 860 as in force 2026-11-21.

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
A De Novo request is received by FDA and is accepted with no additional-information submission. (a) What is the outside time limit for FDA's acceptance notification? (b) What is the outside time limit for FDA's review and issuance of an order granting or declining the request?

2. ANSWERS
(a) Acceptance notification: 15 days after FDA receives the De Novo request. Authority: 21 CFR 860.230(a) (and the deemed-acceptance backstop at 860.230(b), which uses the same 15-day period).
(b) Review and order granting or declining: 120 days after FDA receives the De Novo request. Authority: 21 CFR 860.240(a).
Both periods run from the same anchor — the date FDA receives the request — not from the date of the acceptance notice. Because no additional information is submitted, the alternative trigger in 860.240(a) ("receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under §860.230") does not apply and does not restart or extend the 120-day period.

3. OPERATIVE TEXT (verbatim, 21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D)
§860.230(a): "The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted."
§860.230(b): "If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA."
§860.240(a): "FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under §860.230. Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under §860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under §860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b)."

4. VERSION IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21
Part 860, Subpart D, as retrieved from the eCFR and from the 2025 printed CFR (title 21, vol. 8, part 860, Subpart D). The source note for §860.240 reads "[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]". The December 4, 2025 amendment is the latest amendment to Subpart D and it precedes 2026-11-21; it modifies §860.240(c) (facility inspection / Quality Management System Regulation cross-reference), not the time limits in §860.230(a)/(b) or §860.240(a). No amendment took effect between 2026-11-21 and the retrieval date that would change either number. The quoted time limits are therefore the limits in force on 2026-11-21.

5. DAY-COUNTING CONVENTION
Both periods are stated in "days." Part 860 defines neither "day" nor any business-day, working-day, or "FDA day" convention, and contains no provision excluding weekends or Federal holidays from these periods. The periods are therefore calendar days. Where FDA intends a non-calendar count, its regulations say so expressly; Part 860 does not. Practical corollary: the day of receipt is not counted (the period begins the day after receipt), and the deadline is the calendar date so computed; Part 860 contains no roll-forward rule, so the conservative reading is that FDA must act by that calendar date even if it is a weekend or holiday.

6. WORKED EXAMPLES (calendar-day arithmetic, day of receipt excluded)
Example A — receipt 2026-11-02.
  • Acceptance notification: 2026-11-02 + 15 days = 2026-11-17.
  • Review and order: 2026-11-02 + 120 days = 2027-03-02 (Nov 30 = day 28; Dec 31 = day 59; Jan 31 = day 90; Feb 28 = day 118; Mar 2 = day 120; 2027 is not a leap year).
Example B — receipt 2026-11-30.
  • Acceptance notification: 2026-11-30 + 15 days = 2026-12-15.
  • Review and order: 2026-11-30 + 120 days = 2027-03-30 (Dec 31 = day 31; Jan 31 = day 62; Feb 28 = day 90; Mar 30 = day 120).

7. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE THE ANSWER
• No tolling or extension provision. Part 860 Subpart D contains no mechanism to pause or extend either period, and no provision for extension by agreement (contrast with programs that expressly permit agreed timelines). The 15- and 120-day figures are outer limits, not performance goals.
• Requester amendments. §860.240(b) permits a requester to supplement or amend a pending request, and §860.240(b)(1) permits FDA to require additional information, but neither provision extends the 120-day period by its terms. In the fact pattern given, no such submission occurs, so the question does not arise.
• Rejection-and-resubmission path. §860.230(c)(3) provides that if FDA refuses to accept and the requester later submits the additional information, "the date of acceptance is the date FDA receives the additional information." That would move the anchor date. It is inapplicable here (request accepted without additional information) and is the single fact that, if it were present, would change the 120-day computation.
• MDUFA performance goals. Agency performance goals for De Novo review are internal targets and are not the regulatory outer limits; they are out of scope and do not modify §860.230 or §860.240.

8. ADJACENT DEADLINE — NOT PART OF THE ANSWER, FLAGGED TO PREVENT CONFUSION
§860.260(a)(2): if FDA grants a De Novo request, it must publish the classification order (including any special controls) in the Federal Register within 30 days after issuance of the granting order. This is a post-order publication deadline; it is not the review-and-order limit and must not be substituted for the 120-day figure.

9. OPERATING PROCEDURE FOR A REQUESTER TRACKING THESE LIMITS
Step 1 — Anchor. Record the FDA receipt date (the date FDA receives the request, not the date of any earlier courier delivery to a different address and not the date of the acceptance letter). This is Day 0.
Step 2 — Acceptance checkpoint. Compute Day 0 + 15 calendar days. If no acceptance notice has issued by that date, treat the request as deemed accepted under §860.230(b) and note that the acceptance date is legally the receipt date.
Step 3 — Order checkpoint. Compute Day 0 + 120 calendar days. That is the outside date for a granting order under §860.260(a) or a declining order under §860.260(b).
Step 4 — Do not re-anchor. Do not restart the 120-day count at the acceptance notice date; doing so would overstate the outside date by the length of the acceptance review (up to 15 days).
Step 5 — Calendar controls. Set internal alerts at Day 10 (acceptance escalation), Day 90 and Day 105 (order escalation), and diarize the Day 120 date as the outside limit.

10. RESIDUAL RISK AND HONEST LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
• The values 15 and 120 are taken verbatim from the regulatory text; no interpretation is required to reach them.
• The one interpretive step is the calendar-day reading in section 5. Part 860 does not define "day." The reading is supported by the absence of any business-day definition or exclusion in Part 860, but it is an inference from silence rather than an express definition, and it is disclosed as such.
• The statutory counterpart in section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act is the authority Part 860 implements; the operative text for this question is the regulation quoted above, and this memorandum does not rest any number on an unverified paraphrase of the statute.

11. VERIFICATION TABLE
  Acceptance notice limit: 15 days — source §860.230(a) — anchor: FDA receipt — ≤ 120 (consistent).
  Review/order limit: 120 days — source §860.240(a) — anchor: FDA receipt — ≥ 15 (consistent); not measured from the acceptance notice.
  Restart trigger: receipt of additional information resulting in acceptance (§860.240(a), §860.230(c)(3)) — not present in the fact pattern — no effect.
  Post-order publication: 30 days after a granting order (§860.260(a)(2)) — separate, downstream, not part of ask 4.

question: Y163
answer:
Regulatory basis: ICH E2A, Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting, Step 4 version dated 27 October 1994, section III.A.1. For fatal or life-threatening, unexpected adverse drug reactions occurring in clinical investigations, the guideline states that regulatory agencies should be notified as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. The E2A time-clock start point is the date the sponsor first receives a case meeting the minimum criteria and the expedited-reporting criteria; that date is day 0. The counting is in calendar days, not business days, and weekends or public holidays do not extend the deadline.

Ask 1 — outer limit for initial notification: 7 calendar days after first knowledge. Measured from day 0, the outer limit is day 7. This is a maximum, not a target: the notification should be made as soon as possible, and earlier submission is preferred.

Ask 2 — constraint if the full period is used: if the sponsor uses the entire 7-day initial window, the initial notification is made on day 7. The follow-up obligation is not open-ended and is not satisfied by the initial report alone. E2A requires the follow-up report, as complete as possible, within 8 additional calendar days. Therefore, when the full initial period is used, the follow-up outer limit is day 7 plus 8 additional calendar days.

Ask 3 — follow-up deadline measured from day 0: day 15. Calculation: day 0 = first knowledge; day 7 = outer limit for the initial notification; day 7 + 8 additional calendar days = day 15. The follow-up report must include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products, to the extent possible.

Illustrative date arithmetic: if day 0 is Monday 1 January, the initial notification is due no later than Monday 8 January (day 7), and the follow-up report is due no later than Tuesday 16 January (day 15).

Important correction: the follow-up is not due one day after the initial deadline. The phrase '8 additional calendar days' means eight further calendar days after the 7-day initial window, producing a total of 15 calendar days from day 0 when the full initial period is used. A one-day follow-up reading would be inconsistent with the E2A text.

Applicability note: this answer is the ICH E2A default for a case that qualifies for the seven-day rule. National or regional requirements may be stricter, may impose different notification channels, or may set separate clocks; the sponsor must confirm the applicable local regulation. For the E2A default itself, the initial outer limit is 7 calendar days and the follow-up outer limit is 15 calendar days from day 0 when the full initial period is used.

Primary source: ICH E2A Step 4, 27 October 1994, section III.A.1, as reproduced in the Health Canada and Anvisa guidance copies and referenced by the European Medicines Agency as CPMP/ICH/377/95.

question: Y164
answer:
ANSWER: The next submission must carry serial number 018.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT
21 CFR 312.23(e) ("Numbering of IND submissions"), quoted verbatim from the supplied eCFR/GovInfo text:

  "Each submission relating to an IND is required to be numbered serially using a single, three-digit serial number. The initial IND is required to be numbered 000; each subsequent submission (e.g., amendment, report, or correspondence) is required to be numbered chronologically in sequence."

Three operative rules follow from that sentence:
  (i) The initial IND is fixed at 000 — it is not "submission 1".
  (ii) Every subsequent submission (amendment, report, or correspondence) gets the next number chronologically — one number per submission, no reuse, no gaps created by withdrawals.
  (iii) The number is a single, three-digit, zero-padded serial.

2. CALCULATION

  Serial 000 .......... initial IND (original application)
  Serial 001 .......... 1st subsequent submission
  Serial 002 .......... 2nd subsequent submission
  ...
  Serial 017 .......... 17th subsequent submission  (last number used)
  Serial 018 .......... NEXT submission  <-- answer

General form: next serial = 000 + (number of subsequent submissions already made) + 1 = 000 + 17 + 1 = 018.

Note on the wording: the prompt says "the initial IND and 17 later submissions." The original is stated separately and is designated 000, so the 17 later submissions are 001-017 and do not include 000. If the 17 had been intended to include the original (i.e., 000-016), the next number would be 017; that reading is excluded by the prompt's phrasing and by 312.23(e), which counts the initial IND as 000 rather than as the first numbered submission.

3. FORMAT OF THE NUMBER AS SUBMITTED
  - Write it as three digits, zero-padded: 018. Not "18", not "180", not "018.0".
  - One serial per submission; do not split a submission across multiple serials or reuse a serial for a resubmission.
  - Place it on Form FDA-1571, field 11 ("Serial Number"), and in the cover letter and eCTD/ESG submission metadata, identically in all locations.
  - Field 11 of Form FDA-1571 as currently published instructs "Serial number: 0000" for the initial IND and "Serial Number: 0001" for the next submission (four characters). That is the form's field-width convention; the regulation requires three digits. In a four-character field, enter 0018; the governing serial number is 018 either way. Do not let the form's four-digit example lead to numbering the file as 0001-0017; the file's serials remain 001-017, next 018.

4. WHY THE 17 ARE ALL IN THE SEQUENCE (no exclusion path)
312.23(e) names "amendment, report, or correspondence" as the categories that are numbered, and says "each submission relating to an IND." The numbered categories therefore include protocol amendments (312.30), information amendments (312.31), IND safety reports and follow-up safety reports (312.32), annual reports (312.33), and general correspondence. Because the prompt states all 17 were "numbered correctly," none of them can have fallen outside that set in a way that would leave the last used serial below 017. Consequently there is no alternative arithmetic: the last used serial is 017.

5. EVENTS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE ANSWER
  - A withdrawn or rejected submission keeps its number; the sequence is chronological, not a count of live documents. The next submission is still 018.
  - An IND placed on inactive status (312.45) or reactivated, or a response to a clinical hold (312.42), is still a numbered submission.
  - A submission that FDA returned without filing still consumed its serial.
  - Duplicate or corrected copies of an already-numbered submission should be submitted under the original serial with a note, not as a new serial — this preserves the 017 high-water mark.

6. VERIFICATION BEFORE THE NEXT SUBMISSION GOES OUT (Regulatory Affairs check)
  a. Confirm the highest serial in the IND file's submission log is 017 and that 001-017 are each represented exactly once with no gaps or duplicates.
  b. Confirm the original IND is recorded as 000.
  c. If any log discrepancy exists, resolve it against FDA's acknowledgment/correspondence for the affected submission before assigning the next number; do not silently renumber.
  d. Assign 018 to the next submission, apply it consistently on Form FDA-1571 field 11, the cover letter, and the electronic submission metadata, and add it to the submission log on the date of submission.

7. RESIDUAL RISK / LIMIT
This answer is correct given the prompt's stipulation that the 17 later submissions were all numbered correctly and sequentially. It cannot detect an actual historical numbering error in the sponsor's file; item 6(a) is the control that would surface one. If the sponsor's log shows a high-water mark other than 017 (for example, a serial assigned to a submission that was never sent, or a submission sent without a serial), the next number is high-water mark + 1, not 018.

question: Y165
answer:
ANSWER (ask 2): No. Under 21 CFR Part 807 subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, the manufacturer of a device that meets the section 520(b) custom-device definition is not required to submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution. Section 807.85(a) exempts such a device from the premarket notification requirements of subpart E, and the 90-day clock in 807.81(a) never starts for an exempt device.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT (as verified for 2026-11-21)

1.1 Duty provision — 21 CFR 807.81(a): 'Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria: (1) ... first time ... (2) ... first time by a person required to register ...'

1.2 Exemption provision — 21 CFR 807.85(a): 'A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. (1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or (2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).'

1.3 Amendment history on the face of 807.85: '[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016]' — the 2016 amendment conformed the regulation to the FDASIA § 617 rewrite of section 520(b) (effective July 9, 2012).

1.4 Statutory anchor — section 520(b) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 360j(b)), which exempts qualifying custom devices from the premarket approval requirement of section 515 and from conformance to mandatory performance standards under section 514, and which is the definition 807.85(a) incorporates by reference.

2. ANALYSIS (steps a reviewer can re-run)

Step 1 — Is there a 90-day duty at all? 807.81(a) imposes the 90-day-before-commercial-distribution submission duty on persons required to register under 807.20 who introduce a device into commercial distribution for the first time. On its face the duty would reach a first-time custom device.

Step 2 — Does subpart E carve the device out? 807.81(a) is expressly subject to 807.81(b), and 807.85(a) is the operative carve-out: a device 'within the meaning of section 520(b)' 'is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart.' 'This subpart' is subpart E, which contains 807.81. The exemption is therefore self-executing on the face of the quoted text and does not depend on the exact wording of 807.81(b); 807.81(b)'s cross-reference to 807.85 is the belt-and-braces confirmation (the full text of 807.81(b) was not in the fetched excerpt, so the answer rests on 807.85(a)'s own words, which are unambiguous).

Step 3 — Does the device fall inside 807.85(a)? Yes, on the stated premise. The question stipulates that the device 'meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b).' That stipulation satisfies the only condition 807.85(a) states. The two indented prongs in 807.85(a) track the two statutory custom-device categories: patient-specific (physician's order names the patient) and physician-specific (sole use by the ordering practitioner, not generally available to or used by others). A device satisfying section 520(b) necessarily falls in one of them.

Step 4 — Result. The 90-day submission duty of 807.81(a) does not apply. The manufacturer may proceed to commercial distribution of the custom device without a 510(k), without waiting 90 days, subject to the residual obligations in section 4 below.

3. WHAT FLIPS THE ANSWER TO 'YES' (the exemption is fact-specific, not device-category-specific)

If any element of section 520(b) fails, 807.85(a) does not apply and 807.81(a) reinstates the 90-day duty. Practical triggers, in the order FDA applies them (Custom Device Exemption guidance, Sept. 2014; FDA Medical Devices FAQ, Q18):
(a) The device is generally available in finished form for purchase or for dispensing on prescription;
(b) The device is offered for commercial distribution through labeling or advertising;
(c) The device is generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians/dentists — i.e., it is not truly physician-specific;
(d) The device is neither made in a specific form for a named patient nor intended to meet the special needs of the ordering practitioner in the course of professional practice;
(e) The device does not 'necessarily deviate' from generally available devices or from an applicable performance standard or PMA requirement in order to comply with the individual practitioner's order;
(f) More than 5 units per year of that device type are distributed under the physician-practice prong — section 520(b)(2)(B) caps that prong at 5 units per year; exceeding the cap removes the device from the exemption;
(g) The device is patient-specific and physician-specific at once — FDA's guidance states a custom device cannot be both patient-centric and physician-centric.
The project brief's assumption 'one device per order, physician-driven ordering' supports prongs (a)-(d) only if the order names the patient or the device is confined to the ordering practitioner's practice; that assumption should be documented per order, not asserted once.

4. WHAT THE EXEMPTION DOES NOT COVER

807.85(a) exempts from premarket notification only. A custom-device manufacturer remains subject to: establishment registration and device listing (21 CFR Part 807 subparts B and C; the guidance lists 'Registration and Listing (21 CFR Part 807)' among requirements not exempted); Quality System regulation including design controls (21 CFR Part 820); Medical Device Reporting (21 CFR Part 803); labeling (21 CFR Part 801); corrections and removals (21 CFR Part 806); and the section 520(b) annual report to FDA on devices distributed under the exemption. Section 520(b) also exempts from PMA and mandatory performance standards, but nothing else.

5. VERIFICATION OF THE 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21' CONSTRAINT (ask 1)

5.1 Sources checked: eCFR Title 21, Part 807, Subpart E (fetched 2026-11-23T11:32:12Z, sha256 c74dcd356a8a); GovInfo CFR 2025 edition, title 21 vol. 8, part 807 subpart E XML (fetched 2026-11-23T11:32:13Z, sha256 e0a4b2568d23). Both render 807.81(a), 807.85(a) and 807.100 identically, character for character, in the passages quoted above.
5.2 Currency: the eCFR is a 'current' snapshot; the annual edition is the 2025 codification. Both carry 807.85's amendment note terminating at 81 FR 70340 (Oct. 12, 2016), i.e., no amendment between the 2025 codification and the 2026-11-23 fetch. The text in force on 2026-11-21 is therefore the version quoted.
5.3 Residual check (do this before relying on the opinion in a submission): search the Federal Register for documents amending 21 CFR 807.81, 807.85 or 807.100 with an effective date on or before 2026-11-21 and a publication date after the 2025 annual edition — the two-day gap between the stated date and the snapshot is the only interval the fetched sources do not close by construction. Nothing in the fetched material suggests such a change, and the exemption has been stable since 2016.

6. CORRECTION TO A PREMISE IN THE PROJECT BRIEF

The brief refers to '21 CFR 807.100(a)(2)' as the provision that 'historically exempted custom devices from premarket notification.' That is wrong and should not be carried into any filing. 807.100 is 'FDA action on a premarket notification'; 807.100(a)(2) is the order declaring a device 'not substantially equivalent' (an NSE). The custom-device exemption is 807.85(a). The only arguably relevant 807.100 provision is 807.100(a)(5), by which FDA may '[a]dvise the applicant that the premarket notification is not required' — a response to a submission that need not have been made, not an exemption. The answer above does not depend on 807.100 at all.

7. SECONDARY POINTS A REVIEWER MAY RAISE

7.1 'Commercial distribution' — 807.81(a) uses the phrase in its regulatory sense (introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce). The answer is the same on either reading: an exempt custom device triggers no 90-day pre-notification obligation, and the phrase is not defined in the quoted subpart E text.
7.2 Other pathways — if the device were class III and not custom, section 515 (PMA) rather than 510(k) would govern; but a genuine custom device is exempt from PMA under section 520(b), so no parallel premarket pathway displaces the answer. If the device is not in fact custom, the 510(k) route (with its 90-day lead time) is the default for class I/II first-time distribution.
7.3 Voluntary submission — a manufacturer may still submit a 510(k) and receive an 807.100(a)(5) 'not required' advice; that is optional and does not create a 90-day obligation.

8. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE FILE

Device meets section 520(b) → 21 CFR 807.85(a) exempts it from subpart E premarket notification → the 90-day requirement of 21 CFR 807.81(a) does not apply → no premarket notification is due before commercial distribution. Document the section 520(b) element-by-element basis (including the 5-units-per-year count where the physician-practice prong is used), and calendar the annual report, registration/listing, QS, MDR, labeling and corrections/removals obligations, which the exemption does not touch.

question: Y166
answer:
## Verdict

**No.** On the CDC page *Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis* (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/, page-dated Apr. 17, 2025; retrieved 2026-11-23T11:35:14Z, sha256 9095c1db7f3e), the stated preference for TB blood tests does **not** apply to a 4-year-old who received BCG. The page's preference is expressly age-gated at 5 years and older; a 4-year-old falls on the other side of that line, and the page's operative recommendation for that child is the TB skin test (TST).

---

## 1. What the page actually says (verbatim, from the page named in the ask)

**Decisive sentence — the blood-test preference:**

> "Only one visit is required to draw blood for the test. **TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.**"

**The page's rule for children under 5:**

> "TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
> **Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age**, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children."

Both passages are from the same page section ("TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])" / "TB skin test (Mantoux tuberculin skin test)") of https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/.

---

## 2. Why the answer is No

The page's preference is a **compound condition**, not a single one:

| Limb of the stated condition | This child | Met? |
|---|---|---|
| 5 years of age and older | 4 years old | **No** (4 < 5) |
| Has received the BCG vaccine | Received BCG | Yes |

A conjunction with one false limb is false. The child satisfies the BCG limb — which is the limb a reader naturally fixates on, because BCG is the reason the preference exists — but not the age limb. **The preference as stated does not reach this child.**

The page then supplies the affirmative rule that does reach him: TST is the recommended method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, with blood testing in that age band framed as a matter of expert/AAP discretion ("some experts use TB blood tests in younger children"), not as CDC's preferred method.

The underlying *rationale* for the preference is age-independent — BCG does not induce false-positive IGRA results, so the BCG problem that muddies TST interpretation simply does not arise with a blood test. But the question asks what the **page states**, not what the biology implies, and the page states the preference with an explicit age floor. Rationale and stated scope diverge here, and the stated scope controls.

---

## 3. Corroboration elsewhere in the same CDC testing section (context, not the basis of the verdict)

- **Tuberculosis Clinical Care for Children** (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html, Apr. 17, 2025): "Health care providers should recommend the TB blood test if a child: **Is five years of age or older** and **Has ever received the BCG vaccine (TB vaccine).** Unlike the TB skin test, TB blood tests are not affected by the BCG vaccine." Same age gate, stated as a bulleted two-part checklist — the cleanest confirmation that the BCG trigger is deliberately paired with a ≥5-year condition.
- **Clinical and Laboratory Diagnosis for Tuberculosis** (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/clinical-and-laboratory-diagnosis.html): "TB blood tests are preferred for: People who have received the BCG vaccine and People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading... **Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age.**" The BCG bullet appears unqualified in isolation, but the same page's child-age sentence immediately follows and constrains it.

## 4. A textual tension the reader should be told about

One sentence on the *Tuberculin Skin Test* subpage (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html) reads **without an age qualifier**:

> "BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. **TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.**"

Taken alone, "including children" could be read as extending the preference to a 4-year-old. It should not be, for three reasons:

1. The ask names the **parent** page, whose sentence carries the explicit "5 years of age and older" qualifier; that is the sentence that answers the question.
2. The same subpage, under "Age," restates the binding rule: "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children." A document does not override its own explicit age rule with a general phrase in an adjacent paragraph.
3. The children's clinical-care page spells out the same two-part condition with the age limb first. Two of three statements are age-gated, and the ungated phrase is a summary sentence, not a rule.

Even on the most generous reading of the subpage sentence, the answer to the question *as posed about the named page* is unchanged: the named page's preference does not apply to a 4-year-old.

---

## 5. Provenance and scope notes

- **Date constraint.** The harness retrieved the page on 2026-11-23T11:35:14Z, i.e. 2 days after the requested date of 2026-11-21. The page carries a revision date of **Apr. 17, 2025** and the same Apr. 17, 2025 date on the companion children's page. question: Y168
answer:
REGULATORY POSITION — 21 CFR PART 50, TEXT IN FORCE 2026-11-21
Subject: Sufficiency of 'minimal risk' as a stand-alone basis for enrolling a subject without informed consent; definition of minimal risk.

=====================================================================
1. SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

(1) Version constraint. The analysis below is against Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21. The operative minimal-risk consent provision, § 50.22, carries the source note '[88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023]' in the eCFR text retrieved 2026-11-23; no later amendment appears in that source note. The text below is therefore the text in force on 2026-11-21.

(2) VERDICT — Is 'the research is minimal risk' alone a sufficient reason to enroll without informed consent? NO.
  - Minimal risk is a NECESSARY condition under § 50.22(a), but it is only one of FIVE conjunctive findings the IRB must make and document.
  - The decision-maker is the IRB 'responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation' — not the investigator. An investigator's own minimal-risk determination has no operative effect.
  - Enrollment may not begin until the IRB has made and documented all five findings and approved the altered/waived consent procedure.
  - Where the research is not minimal risk and is not an emergency, Part 50 supplies no general waiver path for adults; § 50.23 and § 50.24 are the only other consent exceptions, and each has conditions independent of (and in § 50.24's case, largely inconsistent with) a minimal-risk characterization.

(3) VALUE — Definition of minimal risk, § 50.3(k), verbatim:
  'Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.'

=====================================================================
2. CONTROLLING TEXT (QUOTED)
=====================================================================

§ 50.22 Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations (88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023):

'The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation described in this section may approve an informed consent procedure that does not include or that alters some or all of the elements of informed consent set forth in § 50.25(a) and (b), or may waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following:
  (a) The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;
  (b) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration;
  (c) If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format;
  (d) The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects; and
  (e) Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation.'

§ 50.3(k) — quoted in full in section 1(3) above.

§ 50.24(a) (emergency research) — for contrast; note the entry conditions are life-threatening situation, infeasibility of consent, prospect of direct benefit, and impracticability, NOT minimal risk:
  '(1) The human subjects are in a life-threatening situation, available treatments are unproven or unsatisfactory, and the collection of valid scientific evidence ... is necessary to determine the safety and effectiveness of particular interventions.
   (2) Obtaining informed consent is not feasible because: (i) The subjects will not be able to give their informed consent as a result of their medical condition; (ii) The intervention under investigation must be administered before consent from the subjects' legally authorized representatives is feasible; and (iii) There is no reasonable way to identify prospectively the individuals likely to become eligible for participation in the clinical investigation.
   (3) Participation in the research holds out the prospect of direct benefit to the subjects because ... (iii) Risks associated with the investigation are reasonable in relation to what is known about the medical condition of the potential class of subjects, the risks and benefits of standard therapy, if any, and what is known about the risks and benefits of the proposed intervention or activity.
   (4) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the waiver.'

=====================================================================
3. WHY 'SOLELY MINIMAL RISK' FAILS — ELEMENT BY ELEMENT
=====================================================================

Failure A — Conflation of one criterion with the whole test.
§ 50.22(a) is one of five lettered criteria joined by 'and'. A finding of minimal risk with no finding on (b), (c) (when identifiable private information or biospecimens are used), (d) or (e) is not an IRB action under § 50.22 at all; it is an incomplete record. Each of the other four is independently dispositive.

Failure B — Wrong actor.
The regulation vests the authority in 'The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation.' The investigator's belief that a study is minimal risk is an input to IRB review, not a waiver. Enrollment on the investigator's own determination is a consent violation regardless of whether the study is in fact minimal risk.

Failure C — 'Could not practicably be carried out' is a separate, study-specific showing.
Criterion (b) requires that the study could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration. This is not established by the risk level; a minimal-risk study that can practicably be carried out with consent must be carried out with consent. The finding must be documented with study-specific reasoning.

Failure D — Identifiable-information criterion is triggered by data type, not risk.
Criterion (c) applies whenever identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are involved, and requires its own impracticability finding as to the identifiable format. A minimal-risk chart-review study using identifiers still fails § 50.22 if the IRB cannot document (c).

Failure E — Rights-and-welfare finding and debriefing are independent.
Criterion (d) requires an affirmative finding that the waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of subjects; criterion (e) requires post-participation provision of additional pertinent information whenever appropriate.

Failure F — Documentation is an element of the rule, not a nicety.
The text reads 'provided the IRB finds and documents the following.' An undocumented finding is not a finding for purposes of § 50.22.

Failure G — Scope limit.
§ 50.22 authorizes the IRB to approve a consent procedure that omits or alters elements of § 50.25(a) and (b), or to waive the requirement to obtain informed consent. It does not, on its face, address documentation of consent under § 50.27; documentation waiver is a separate question (see 21 CFR 56.109(c), to be confirmed against current text with the reviewing IRB). Do not treat a § 50.22 approval as automatically waiving signed documentation.

Conclusion on Ask 2: the investigator's statement is incorrect as stated. The accurate statement is: 'This clinical investigation may enroll subjects without informed consent only if the reviewing IRB finds and documents all five § 50.22 criteria, one of which is that the investigation involves no more than minimal risk.'

=====================================================================
4. THE § 50.3(k) DEFINITION — PARSED
=====================================================================

Component 1 — Two dimensions, both bounded: 'the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research.' Both likelihood and severity must be assessed; a low-probability high-severity harm is not rescued by low probability alone, and a high-probability trivial discomfort is not condemned by frequency alone.

Component 2 — 'anticipated in the research': the assessment covers the harms the research itself adds, judged prospectively.

Component 3 — The comparator: 'not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.' Two alternative benchmarks: (i) ordinary daily life, or (ii) routine physical or psychological examinations/tests. The phrase 'in and of themselves' directs the comparison to the harm of the research procedures, not to the subject's underlying disease or baseline condition.

Component 4 — It is a ceiling, not a floor, and not zero risk. 'Not greater than' permits risk equal to the benchmark. Minimal risk is not synonymous with 'no risk' and is not a statement that the research is beneficial or trivial.

Component 5 — 'Harm or discomfort' includes psychological and social discomfort, not only physical injury.

Component 6 — Location and function. The definition sits in the general definitions of Subpart A (§ 50.3(k)) and therefore governs every use of the term in Part 50, including § 50.22(a) and § 50.25(a)(6). The wording is materially identical to the Common Rule definition, but the operative waiver criteria are those of Part 50; do not import HHS-specific interpretations wholesale without checking FDA's position.

Component 7 — Other regulatory work the term does. Minimal risk also controls § 50.25(a)(6): the explanation of compensation and available medical treatment for injury is required only 'For research involving more than minimal risk.' A minimal-risk finding therefore changes the required consent content as well as enabling a § 50.22 request — a second reason the finding must be correct and documented.

=====================================================================
5. THE OTHER PART 50 CONSENT EXCEPTIONS — AND WHY MINIMAL RISK DOES NOT SUBSTITUTE FOR THEM
=====================================================================

Pathway | Governing section | Risk-level requirement | Other conditions that dominate
---|---|---|---
Minimal-risk waiver/alteration | § 50.22 | No more than minimal risk (required) | Impracticability; identifiable-data impracticability; no adverse effect on rights/welfare; debriefing when appropriate; IRB finding and documentation
Emergency research | § 50.24 | None stated as minimal risk; risks must be 'reasonable in relation to' condition, standard therapy, and the intervention | Life-threatening situation; unproven/unsatisfactory available treatments; consent infeasible on all three grounds; prospect of direct benefit; impracticability; concurrence of a licensed physician IRB member/consultant not otherwise participating; community consultation and public disclosure; independent data monitoring where required
Emergency use (single patient / narrow) | § 50.23 | Not a minimal-risk pathway | Life-threatening situation, no standard acceptable treatment, insufficient time to obtain IRB approval, physician concurrence, and prompt IRB reporting — confirm current paragraph structure against the text in force

Key point for the investigator: § 50.24 does not require minimal risk and cannot be satisfied by showing minimal risk; conversely, a study that is minimal risk but not an emergency must proceed under § 50.22, and a study that is neither minimal risk nor an emergency has no waiver pathway under Part 50 for adults.

=====================================================================
6. PROCEDURE — WHAT MUST HAPPEN BEFORE ANY SUBJECT IS ENROLLED WITHOUT CONSENT
=====================================================================

Step 1. Confirm the activity is a 'clinical investigation' within § 50.3(c) (test article plus human subjects, subject to § 505(i)/§ 520(g) prior-submission requirements, or results intended for submission to or inspection by FDA). If it is not, Part 50 does not apply and a different framework governs.

Step 2. Identify the pathway. Minimal-risk, non-emergency → § 50.22. Emergency → § 50.24 (or § 50.23 for the narrow single-use case). Do not proceed if no pathway fits.

Step 3. Have the IRB of record make each finding in writing, separately, using the regulatory language:
  (a) 'The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects' — with the § 50.3(k) comparator identified (daily life or routine examinations/tests) and the specific procedures assessed.
  (b) 'The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration' — with the study-specific reason (e.g., the only practicable design requires no prospective contact; the population cannot be identified prospectively; consent would destroy the scientific validity of the measurement).
  (c) Where identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are used: 'The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format.'
  (d) 'The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects.'
  (e) 'Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation' — record the debriefing plan or the basis for finding debriefing not appropriate.

Step 4. Record the approval of the altered/waived consent procedure in the IRB minutes and the approval letter; specify exactly which § 50.25(a) and (b) elements are waived or altered (all or a listed subset).

Step 5. Resolve documentation of consent separately (§ 50.27; and see 21 CFR 56.109(c) on waiver of signed documentation). Do not assume § 50.22 resolves it.

Step 6. Confirm no overlay adds requirements: applicable state law; institutional policy; for children, Subpart D (§§ 50.50–50.56) permission from parents and assent from the child under § 50.3(n)/(r), which a § 50.22 waiver does not displace; population-specific subparts and state law for pregnant women, neonates, and prisoners.

Step 7. Do not enroll until Steps 3–6 are complete. Retain the documented findings for inspection.

=====================================================================
7. MODEL IRB FINDING LANGUAGE (ADOPTABLE)
=====================================================================

'The IRB finds and documents, pursuant to 21 CFR 50.22, that: (a) the clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects, because [procedures] present a probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests; (b) the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver/alteration, because [reason]; (c) [where applicable] the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using identifiable private information/biospecimens in an identifiable format, because [reason]; (d) the waiver/alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects, because [reason]; and (e) [debriefing will be provided as follows / debriefing is not appropriate because].' 

=====================================================================
8. COMMON ERRORS THIS MEMO IS INTENDED TO FORECLOSE
=====================================================================

- Treating 'minimal risk' as a self-executing authorization. It is not; § 50.22 requires four additional findings, made by the IRB, and documented.
- Treating the Common Rule's waiver criteria as interchangeable with Part 50's. The criteria are now closely aligned, but the operative authority for an FDA-regulated clinical investigation is Part 50, and the FDA text controls.
- Assuming § 50.24 can be used because the study is low risk. § 50.24 turns on life-threatening circumstances and prospect of direct benefit, not on risk level.
- Overlooking § 50.25(a)(6): a minimal-risk determination also removes the obligation to give the injury-compensation explanation, so an erroneous minimal-risk finding has consent-content consequences beyond the waiver itself.
- Overlooking Subpart D and state law, which can defeat a waiver that Part 50 would otherwise permit.

=====================================================================
9. SOURCES AND VERSION CONTROL
=====================================================================

- 21 CFR 50.22 — eCFR (retrieved 2026-11-23T11:39:26Z; sha256 8f4718b5053d) and 21 CFR Part 50 Subpart B (sha256 9ccc0f664572); source note [88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023].
- 21 CFR 50.3(k) — eCFR (sha256 0ec2ca722aac) and CFR-2025-title21-vol1 XML (sha256 fbc233f28550); the two sources agree verbatim.
- 21 CFR 50.24 — eCFR (sha256 721cc8b321ca).
- Provisions referenced but not quoted from a fetched source (§ 50.20 cross-reference list, § 50.27 documentation, 21 CFR 56.109(c), Subpart D sections, § 50.23 paragraph structure) are identified as items to confirm against the text in force; none of them affects the answers to the three asks.

Source: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics, 2024 edition, '30. Cosmic Rays' (S. Navas et al., Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024); review written October 2023).

Finding: The 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review defines ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) by an energy threshold of 10^18 eV, i.e. 1 EeV. The review expresses the boundary as cosmic rays 'above 10^18 eV.'

Inclusive/exclusive verdict: The threshold is exclusive. The wording 'above 10^18 eV' means E > 10^18 eV; a cosmic ray with energy exactly 10^18 eV is not included by the stated definition. question: Y177

## 1. Answer

Per NASA's errata sheet for NTRS 19770009539 (*U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976*):

- **Enter S = 110.4 K.** (The document's Table 2, Category II Constants, footnote 3 prints `S = 110 K`.)
- **The document's value was too small by 0.4 K** (0.4 kelvin, an additive shortfall, *not* a factor; 110 + 0.4 = 110.4).

Relative shortfall: 0.4/110 = 0.36 %. Resulting error in computed dynamic viscosity: 0.4/(T + 110.4) ≈ **0.10 % at 288.15 K**, growing to ≈0.13 % at 200 K and shrinking to ≈0.04 % at 1000 K.

## 2. Source and exact wording

Errata sheet distributed with NTRS 19770009539 (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf), authored by Yekta Gursel, Ph.D., dated Thursday, January 08, 2015, addressed to NASA HQ-STI-INFODESK, subject "Re: NASA STI Order D-30869". Item 2 under "the rest of the errors I have found in Table 2, B. Category II Constants, on Page 2":

> "2) The value for Sutherland's constant S is too small by 0.4. It should be 110.4 Kelvin."

The document text being corrected (Table 2, footnote 3, page 2):

> "The Sutherland constant, S = 110 K, (Hilsenrath et al., 1955) is a constant in the empirical expression for dynamic viscosity."

The formula the constant belongs to (same footnote block; β = 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^1/2)):

    μ = β · T^(3/2) / (T + S)

Corroboration that 110.4 K is the physically correct value (the printed 110 K is a truncation): the document's own cited source, Hilsenrath et al. (1955), gives 110.4 K; the MATLAB Aerospace Blockset ISA Atmosphere Model documents `S — Sutherland temperature, 110.4 K (default)`; COMSOL's table lists Air S = 111 K (rounded). The errata correction is therefore consistent with independent references and should be adopted without further justification.

**Scope note — do not conflate errata items.** The same errata sheet lists four other, unrelated defects: (a) R* on page 2 Table 2 differs from R* on page 3 by a factor of 10^6 (page 3 value is correct); (b) r0 (Earth mean radius) too large by 1000 in km; (c) sigma (mean effective collision diameter) too large by 10^9 in m; (d) Table III thermal-conductivity column 8 too small by 1000 (equation 53 itself is correct). This change request concerns **item (2), S only**. Items (a), (b), (c), (d) are separate defect tickets; if the same code hard-codes any of those constants, raise them separately rather than folding them into this patch.

## 3. Unit handling — how S must be entered

S is an *absolute temperature* in the Sutherland denominator and must be entered in the same temperature scale used for T in the code. It is independent of the viscosity unit system (SI vs cgs vs English); only β carries the viscosity units.

| Code temperature scale | Enter S as | Shortfall was | β (for reference) |
|---|---|---|---|
| K (SI; β = 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^1/2)) | **110.4 K** | **0.4 K** | 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^1/2) |
| K with cgs viscosity (g/(cm·s) = P) | 110.4 K | 0.4 K | 1.458e-5 g/(cm·s·K^1/2) |
| °R (English; μ in lb/(ft·s)) | **198.72 °R** (110.4 × 1.8) | **0.72 °R** (0.4 × 1.8) | 7.3034e-7 lb/(ft·s·°R^1/2) |
| °C | invalid — S is absolute | — | — |

Do **not** convert S by a viscosity factor. A 10×/1000× "fix" is wrong here; the errata says the shortfall is 0.4, an additive amount, and that the correct value is 110.4.

## 4. Code change

### 4.1 Constant definition (primary edit)

```diff
--- a/atmosphere/constants.py
+++ b/atmosphere/constants.py
@@
-# Sutherland constant, U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, Table 2, Cat. II, p.2
-SUTHERLAND_S = 110.0        # K
+# Sutherland constant, U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, Table 2, Cat. II, p.2.
+# The printed 110 K is too small by 0.4 K; corrected per the NASA NTRS
+# 19770009539 errata sheet (item 2): S = 110.4 K.
+# Source: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf
+SUTHERLAND_S = 110.4        # K  (errata: was 110 K, too small by 0.4 K)
```

If the constant is a configuration value rather than a literal, change the shipped default the same way:

```diff
- sutherland_temperature: 110.0   # K
+ sutherland_temperature: 110.4   # K  (NTRS 19770009539 errata item 2)
```

If the code carries °R internally:

```diff
- SUTHERLAND_S_R = 198.0     # deg R  (== 110.0 K)
+ SUTHERLAND_S_R = 198.72    # deg R  (== 110.4 K, per NTRS 19770009539 errata item 2)
```

### 4.2 Guard so the change is auditable and idempotent

```python
# atmosphere/viscosity.py
from .constants import SUTHERLAND_S, BETA

_ERRATA_S_K = 110.4  # NTRS 19770009539 errata, item 2
assert abs(SUTHERLAND_S - _ERRATA_S_K) < 1e-9, (
    f"Sutherland S = {SUTHERLAND_S} K does not match the errata value "
    f"{_ERRATA_S_K} K; see NTRS 19770009539 errata sheet, item 2."
)

def dynamic_viscosity(T):
    """Sutherland dynamic viscosity, US Std Atm 1976.
    mu = beta * T**1.5 / (T + S), T in K, S = 110.4 K (errata-corrected).
    """
    return BETA * T**1.5 / (T + SUTHERLAND_S)
```

If the code uses the reference-state form `μ = μ_ref (T/T_ref)^1.5 (T_ref + S)/(T + S)`, only S changes; μ_ref = 1.716e-5 kg/(m·s) at T_ref = 273.15 K is unaffected.

## 5. Verification

Post-change regression values from `μ = 1.458e-6 · T^1.5 / (T + 110.4)` (kg/(m·s)). Tolerance 1e-9 relative; these are closed-form, not measured.

| T (K) | μ, S = 110.4 K (new) | μ, S = 110 K (old) | Δμ | Δrel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 200.00 | 1.328558e-5 | 1.330272e-5 | +1.71e-8 | 0.129 % |
| 216.65 | 1.421653e-5 | 1.423389e-5 | +1.74e-8 | 0.122 % |
| 288.15 | 1.789386e-5 | 1.791185e-5 | +1.80e-8 | 0.100 % |
| 500.00 | 2.691070e-5 | 2.692968e-5 | +1.90e-8 | 0.070 % |
| 1000.00 | 4.152727e-5 | 4.154234e-5 | +1.51e-8 | 0.036 % |

Sea-level sanity check: μ(288.15 K) = 1.7894e-5 kg/(m·s), matching the standard sea-level value quoted in the 1976 atmosphere tables (1.7894e-5). The old value gave 1.7912e-5, i.e. 0.10 % high.

English-unit check: μ(518.67 °R) = 7.3034e-7 × 518.67^1.5 / (518.67 + 198.72) = 1.2027e-5 lb/(ft·s), which equals 1.7894e-5 kg/(m·s) × 0.671969 — the two unit paths agree, confirming S = 198.72 °R is the correct entry in that system.

Test to add:

```python
def test_sutherland_constant_is_errata_corrected():
    assert SUTHERLAND_S == 110.4          # K

def test_viscosity_at_sea_level():
    assert abs(dynamic_viscosity(288.15) - 1.789386e-5) < 1e-11

def test_viscosity_monotonic_and_positive():
    ts = [200.0, 216.65, 288.15, 500.0, 1000.0]
    mus = [dynamic_viscosity(t) for t in ts]
    assert all(m > 0 for m in mus)
    assert all(b > a for a, b in zip(mus, mus[1:]))
```

## 6. Regression impact and re-baselining

- Every output that consumes dynamic viscosity shifts by at most ≈0.13 % (largest at the cold tropopause, smallest aloft); density, pressure and temperature are unaffected because S enters only the viscosity/conductivity branch.
- Reynolds number scales as 1/μ, so Re shifts by ≈0.10 % at sea level. Any stored baseline that asserts Re, drag, boundary-layer height or convective coefficient to tighter than 0.2 % must be re-baselined; tolerances looser than 0.2 % will pass unchanged.
- Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ shifts by the same relative amount.
- Do **not** touch the thermal-conductivity Sutherland constant in the same edit. Its constant is a separate quantity (the errata's thermal-conductivity finding concerns Table III scaling by 1000, not S_k); changing it would be an unrequested behaviour change.

## 7. Change-record text

question: Y179
answer:
# Verdict and stated region

**Ask 1 — Does the stated validity region of Eq. (34.5) support evaluating it at βγ = 0.01 and claiming the review's few-percent accuracy?  →  NO.**

**Ask 2 — βγ region over which the review states that accuracy:  0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000**  (dimensionless; both limits are stated by the review to be Z-dependent).

βγ = 0.01 lies one full decade *below* the stated lower bound. It is outside the region, not at its edge.

---

## 1. Primary source, quoted verbatim

From *34. Passage of Particles Through Matter*, in S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024), p. 5, immediately following Eq. (34.5):

> "Eq. (34.5) is valid in the region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent. At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron "speed," and at βγ ∼ 1000 radiative effects begin to be important (Sec. 34.6). Both limits are Z dependent. A minor dependence on M at high energies is introduced through Wmax, but for all practical purposes the stopping power in a given material is a function of β alone. Small corrections are discussed in Sec. 34.2.6."

**Provenance.** Two independently fetched copies of the same review agree word-for-word on this sentence:

| Copy | Footer date | sha256 (prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| `pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf` | 25th March, 2025 | `1b328278e835` |
| `pdg.lbl.gov/2026/download/rpp-2025/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf` | 31st May, 2024 | `3ead731273e0` |

The edition ambiguity raised in the plan is therefore **closed**: the accuracy statement is identical in both dated renderings, so the verdict does not depend on which one the analyst reads.

**Rendering note (disclosed, not glossed).** The PDF text layer extracts the relation as a period — "0.1 . βγ . 1000". That glyph is PDG's *≲* (lesssim: "approximately less than or of order"), not a strict inequality and not a multiplication dot. I have restored ≲ above and it should be quoted that way. The softness is an order-of-magnitude caveat *at the edge* of the interval; it cannot stretch a bound of 0.1 down to 0.01. The answer is insensitive to whether one reads the bound as strict or soft.

---

## 2. Why the answer is No — from the review's own sentences

The quoted passage excludes the proposed use three separate ways, and any one of them is sufficient:

1. **Categorical.** 0.01 < 0.1. The formula's validity interval is stated to begin at 0.1; βγ = 0.01 is a decade below it.
2. **Physical, in the review's own justification.** The review grounds the lower bound as the point where "the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron 'speed.'" At βγ = 0.01 (β = 0.0099995) the projectile is ten times slower still — deep in the adiabatic / strong-coupling regime, where the first Born approximation on which Eq. (34.5) rests is not merely inaccurate but inapplicable (§3 below quantifies this).
3. **The escape hatch does not reach.** The only extension offered is "Small corrections are discussed in Sec. 34.2.6." At βγ = 0.01 the corrections to the Bethe form (shell, Barkas–Andersen, Bloch, effective charge / charge state, nuclear stopping) are O(10–100 %) — they are not small corrections, they are the physics.

Note also that the review says **"Both limits are Z dependent."** Whoever quotes the interval must carry that qualifier: the 0.1 lower bound is not a universal constant, it shifts with the material. But no Z shifts it down to 0.01.

---

## 3. Quantitative check at βγ = 0.01

### 3.1 Kinematics

With βγ = 0.01: β = 0.00999950, γ = 1.0000500, β² = 9.9990 × 10⁻⁵, **β²γ² = 1.0000 × 10⁻⁴**.

Maximum energy transfer in PDG Eq. (34.5), W_max = 2m_ec²β²γ² / (1 + 2γm_e/M + (m_e/M)²):

- proton: **W_max = 102.1 eV**
- corresponding kinetic energies: p 46.9 keV, μ 5.28 keV, π 6.98 keV.

So the analyst is working at tens of keV per unit charge. (For e± the review's formula and its accuracy claim do not apply at all — different W_max, Møller/Bhabha, bremsstrahlung; the passage treats electrons separately.)

### 3.2 The bracket of Eq. (34.5) collapses

Write the PDG bracket as

  B ≡ ½ ln( 2 m_e c² β²γ² W_max / I² ) − β² − δ(βγ)/2 ,   with δ → 0 at low βγ,

so the log numerator at βγ = 0.01 is fixed:

  2 m_e c² β²γ² · W_max = (1.0220 × 10⁻⁴ MeV)(1.0210 × 10⁻⁴ MeV) = **1.0435 × 10⁻⁸ MeV²**.

Everything then hinges on I², and the logarithm is small enough that it has no dynamic range left:

| Material | I (eV) | I² (MeV²) | argument | ½ ln(·) | B = ½ln − β² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H₂ | 19.2 | 3.686e-10 | 28.31 | +1.672 | **+1.672** |
| He | 41.8 | 1.747e-9 | 5.973 | +0.894 | **+0.894** |
| C (graphite) | 78 | 6.084e-9 | 1.715 | +0.270 | **+0.270** |
| water (liquid) | 79.7 | 6.352e-9 | 1.643 | +0.248 | **+0.248** |
| air | 85.7 | 7.344e-9 | 1.421 | +0.176 | **+0.176** |
| Al | 166 | 2.756e-8 | 0.3786 | −0.486 | **−0.486** |
| Si | 173 | 2.993e-8 | 0.3487 | −0.527 | **−0.527** |
| Fe | 286 | 8.180e-8 | 0.1276 | −1.030 | **−1.030** |
| Pb | 823 | 6.773e-7 | 0.01541 | −2.087 | **−2.087** |

**Sign-flip threshold:** B = 0 when I = 1.0214 × 10⁻⁴ MeV = **102.1 eV**. For every material with I > 102 eV — Al, Si, Ar, Fe, Cu, Pb, and most structural and detector materials — the uncorrected Eq. (34.5) returns a **negative mass stopping power** at βγ = 0.01. An expression that returns a negative number for the analyst's actual material cannot be "few percent accurate."

**Error budget already blown by I alone.** Since ∂B/∂ln I = −1 exactly, the relative error in dE/dx from an uncertainty in the mean excitation energy is (ΔI/I)/|B|:

| Material | B | 1 % error in I → error in dE/dx |
|---|---|---|
| C | 0.270 | 3.7 % |
| water | 0.248 | 4.0 % |
| air | 0.176 | 5.7 % |
| Al | −0.486 | sign flip |

A *one-percent* uncertainty in a single tabulated input consumes the entire "few percent" budget at βγ = 0.01, leaving nothing for the correction terms the review assumes are applied.

**Born criterion.** The Bethe form requires η ≡ Zα/β ≪ 1. At β = 0.0099995, η = 0.7298 Z:

| Z | 1 | 6 | 13 | 26 | 82 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| η | 0.73 | 4.4 | 9.5 | 20 | 60 |

η ≪ 1 fails for **every** material, including hydrogen. This is the quantitative content of the review's own sentence about atomic electron speed.

**Corrections that are no longer small at βγ = 0.01** (each individually comparable to or larger than B itself): shell correction (large for medium/heavy Z at β ≈ 0.01); Barkas–Andersen (∝ Z³) and Bloch (∝ Z⁴); low-energy effective charge — at 47 keV/u an ion is not fully stripped, so the z² scaling of Eq. (34.5) is wrong by a large factor for anything heavier than a proton; nuclear stopping, negligible for 47 keV protons in light materials but a large fraction for heavier projectiles. Below roughly β ≈ 0.05–0.1 the standard treatment is Lindhard–Scharff or empirical ZBL/Anderson–Ziegler, or tabulated data — not bare Bethe.

**Robustness to the β vs βγ reading.** If the analyst actually meant β = 0.01 rather than βγ = 0.01, then βγ = 0.0100005 — the conclusion is unchanged. Nothing in this answer is sensitive to that distinction.

---

## 4. What the analyst should write instead

**Do not** write: "using PDG Eq. (34.5), accurate to a few percent [Ref. PDG 2024], we obtain dE/dx at βγ = 0.01."

**Do** write one of these, quoting the region rather than paraphrasing it:

> *Option A (evaluate outside the region, using a source that covers it):*
> "The mean electronic mass stopping power at βγ = 0.01 was taken from NIST PSTAR/ASTAR [or SRIM, or Lindhard–Scharff] for [material]. PDG 2024 Eq. (34.5) is stated to be 'valid in the region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent' [S. Navas et al., Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), Eq. (34.5) and following text], with both limits Z-dependent; βγ = 0.01 lies below that region, so no PDG accuracy claim is made here."

> *Option B (if Eq. (34.5) must be shown for context):*
> "For reference, PDG Eq. (34.5) evaluated at βγ = 0.01 gives [value], which is outside the formula's stated validity region (0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000, few-percent accuracy, both limits Z-dependent) and is quoted only to show where the extrapolation fails; the adopted value is [PSTAR/SRIM value]."

**Decisive one-line check the analyst can run in a minute:** evaluate Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01 for their material and compare with PSTAR/ASTAR (or SRIM) at the same kinetic energy (46.9 keV for a proton). The uncorrected formula is off by a factor of order several — and for I > 102 eV it is not even positive. That comparison, not a literature argument, is what should be filed with the analysis note.

---

## 5. Conditions bundled with the "few percent" — carry these whenever the region is quoted

1. The claim is for the **mean electronic (ionization + atomic excitation) mass stopping power**, MeV g⁻¹ cm², with the symbol definitions of PDG Table 34.1. It is **not** a guarantee for the most-probable energy loss or for straggling in thin absorbers.
2. It is **not** a per-point error bound; it is a statement that the formula reproduces measured mean stopping power to a few percent over that interval. Accuracy degrades toward the low edge and is Z-dependent there.
3. Radiative losses are excluded above βγ ≈ 1000, and mass scaling of dE/dx and range "is valid for the electronic losses described by the Bethe equation, but not for radiative losses."
4. The density-effect term δ(βγ) is part of Eq. (34.5); the "small corrections" of Sec. 34.2.6 are assumed applied.
5. **Both limits are Z dependent** — quote that clause with the interval.

---

## 6. Bottom line

βγ = 0.01 is outside the region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 by a decade. The review's few-percent accuracy statement does not transfer to it under any reading of the bound, for any material, and at that point the uncorrected formula is not merely imprecise but structurally wrong (negative for I > 102 eV; Born parameter η = 0.73 Z ≫ 1). The analyst may of course *evaluate* Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01 for illustration, but must not attach the review's accuracy claim to the result; the number must come from PSTAR/ASTAR, SRIM, Lindhard–Scharff, or equivalent, and the PDG region should be quoted verbatim with its Z-dependence.

## Source and version check (ask 1)

The paper is **Planck Collaboration, 'Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters'**, arXiv:1807.06209. The arXiv metadata states: submitted 17 Jul 2018; last revised **9 Aug 2021 (this version, v4)**; journal reference **A&A 641, A6 (2020)**. All statements below are therefore tied to **v4**, not an earlier or later version.

## Ask 2 — does the BAO-combined result quote a measured value for Σmν?

**No.** In v4 the BAO-combined neutrino-mass result is quoted as a **one-sided upper limit**, not as a measured non-zero value with a central value and uncertainty. The paper does not report a result of the form `Σmν = x ± y` from Planck+BAO. It reports limits such as:

- `Σmν < 0.16 eV (95 %, Planck TT+lowE+BAO)` — Eq. 62a
- `Σmν < 0.13 eV (95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+BAO)` — Eq. 62b
- `Σmν < 0.13 eV (95 %, Planck TT+lowE+lensing+BAO)` — Eq. 63a
- `Σmν < 0.12 eV (95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO)` — Eq. 63b

The conclusions state: `Allowing for a free degenerate active neutrino mass, and combining with BAO measurements, we obtain the tight 95 % constraint on the sum of the masses Σmν < 0.12 eV.` This is an upper bound; the data are consistent with zero mass and no detection is claimed.

## Ask 3 — what constraint does it give?

The headline BAO-combined constraint in v4 is:

**Σmν < 0.12 eV at 95% CL for Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO.**

That is the value to quote for 'the result combining with BAO'. The paper also quotes the baseline `Planck TT+lowE+BAO` limit as `Σmν < 0.16 eV (95%)`; if the report specifically means the baseline TT+lowE+BAO combination rather than the full Planck+BAO headline, use `< 0.16 eV`. In either case it is an upper limit, not a measured value. The paper's tightest quoted BAO-combined limit is the `< 0.12 eV` result above.

## Ask 4 — confidence level assigned to upper limits

The upper limits are quoted at **95% confidence level (95% CL)**. All BAO-combined neutrino-mass limits above carry `95 %`, and the abstract's upper limits are at 95% CL. No 68% CL is used for these neutrino-mass upper limits.

## Citation-ready sentence

`Planck Collaboration, Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters, arXiv:1807.06209v4, A&A 641, A6 (2020): combining Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing with BAO gives Σmν < 0.12 eV at 95% CL; this is an upper limit, not a measured non-zero value.`

question: Y182
answer:
DELIVERABLE — δ-ray rarity illustration in the 2024 PDG 'Passage of Particles Through Matter' review, and the average number of Te > 10 keV collisions in 90 cm of argon gas.

=====================================================================
1. THE QUOTED ILLUSTRATION (Ask 1)
=====================================================================
Source: PDG 2024 review 'Passage of Particles Through Matter' (rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf), Section 34.2.7 'Energetic knock-on electrons (δ rays)', immediately following Eq. (34.9). Verbatim:

  "δ rays of even modest energy are rare. For a β ≈ 1 particle, for example, on
   average only one collision with Te > 10 keV will occur along a path length of
   90 cm of argon gas [1]."

Key points about the illustration as given:
- It is a sentence in the text, not a numbered figure or table. There is no 'Figure 34.x' for δ-ray rarity; the only nearby display equation is Eq. (34.9), the differential δ-ray production spectrum.
- The wording is deliberately order-of-magnitude: 'on average only one collision'. The review does not quote 1.0, 1.1 or an uncertainty; it uses the example to make the qualitative point that hard δ rays are rare compared with the ~10^4–10^5 soft collisions per cm that dominate dE/dx.
- The reference tag [1] is the review's standard citation for the collision formalism (Rossi, High-Energy Particles), i.e. the statement is presented as a standard textbook illustration, not a new calculation.
- The same sentence appears identically in the 2022 and 2023 revisions of the review (verified), so it is a long-standing stable example — safe to cite across detector-physics documents.
- The primary is specified only as 'β ≈ 1' and (by the surrounding section's 'charge ze' convention) singly charged, z = 1; the collision count scales as z².

=====================================================================
2. THE NUMBER (Ask 2)
=====================================================================
Average number of collisions with Te > 10 keV along 90 cm of argon gas for a β ≈ 1, z = 1 particle:

    N(Te > 10 keV; 90 cm Ar) = 1   (as stated by the 2024 PDG review)

Use the value 1 for the background budget, with the understanding that it is an order-unity illustrative figure (see the derivation below, which gives 1.11 — the same number rounded to 'only one').

=====================================================================
3. INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK FROM THE REVIEW'S OWN Eq. (34.9)
=====================================================================
This confirms the quoted 'one' and pins down the (otherwise unstated) gas conditions — important, because the answer is density-dependent.

Eq. (34.9):  d²N/(dT dx) = (1/2) K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) F(T)/T²,  with x in g/cm², T in MeV.

Integrate from Tmin = 10 keV = 0.010 MeV to Wmax, taking F(T) ≈ 1 (valid for T ≪ Wmax; the spin-1/2 form F = 1 − β²T/Wmax is within 10^-3 of unity here):

    N = (1/2) K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) ρL [ 1/Tmin − 1/Wmax ]

Inputs:
    K        = 4π N_A r_e² m_e c² = 0.307075 MeV mol^-1 cm²
    z        = 1
    Z/A (Ar)= 18 / 39.948 = 0.4506 mol^-1
    β        = 1  (β ≈ 1; 1/β² = 1)
    ρ (Ar gas, STP) = 1.784e-3 g/cm³
    L        = 90 cm  →  ρL = 0.16056 g/cm²
    Tmin     = 0.010 MeV → 1/Tmin = 100 MeV^-1
    1/Wmax   ≈ 0 for β ≈ 1 and any heavy primary (e.g. muon at γ = 100: Wmax ≈ 10.2 GeV → 1/Wmax ≈ 1e-4 MeV^-1, i.e. <0.1% correction)

    N = 0.5 × 0.307075 × 1 × 0.4506 × 1 × 0.16056 × 100
      = 0.15354 × 0.4506 × 0.16056 × 100
      = 1.11

Result: N ≈ 1.11 → 'on average only one collision', exactly as the review states.
The agreement also fixes the implied gas condition: STP argon (ρ ≈ 1.78e-3 g/cm³). This matters — for liquid argon (ρ = 1.40 g/cm³) the same integral gives ≈ 870 collisions per 90 cm, which would be irreconcilable with the quoted sentence. Do not apply the review's '1' to a liquid-argon or high-pressure gas volume without rescaling (Section 4).

=====================================================================
4. SCALING LAW FOR THE BACKGROUND BUDGET
=====================================================================
From the same integral, the review's example generalises to:

    N(Te > 10 keV) = 1.11 × z² × (ρ/ρ_Ar,STP) × (L/90 cm) × [1 − 0.010 MeV / Wmax]

with ρ/ρ_Ar,STP = (P/1 atm)(273.15 K / T) for an ideal gas. Practical cases:
    - 1 atm, 293 K, 90 cm, z=1, β≈1 : N ≈ 1.03
    - 10 atm, 90 cm                        : N ≈ 10.3
    - 1 atm, 1 m                           : N ≈ 1.14
    - liquid argon (1.40 g/cm³), 90 cm     : N ≈ 870
    - z = 2 (e.g. alpha, lightly ionised ion): N × 4

=====================================================================
5. STATISTICAL FORM FOR BUDGETING (fluctuations, not just the mean)
=====================================================================
Hard δ-ray production is a rare, independent process, so the count per traversal is Poisson with λ ≈ 1.1:
    P(0)    = e^-1.11          = 0.33
    P(1)    = λ e^-λ           = 0.37
    P(2)    = 0.20
    P(3)    = 0.075
    P(≥1)   = 0.67
    P(≥3)   = 0.10
Consequences for detector-background budgeting:
- Two thirds of β ≈ 1 tracks through 90 cm of argon at STP produce at least one >10 keV δ ray; one third produce none. A per-event budget must not assume 'always zero' or 'always one'.
- The δ ray is emitted at a small angle, cos θ = (Te/pe)(pmax/Wmax) (Eq. 34.10); for Te ≫ m_e c² it is forward-peaked, so a 10 keV δ ray (Te/m_e c² ≈ 0.02) is emitted at up to ~90° — treat it as an isotropic point of local charge deposition, not as part of the primary track.
- Each 10–100 keV δ ray deposits its energy within a few mm in argon gas at STP (range of a 10 keV electron in Ar at STP ≈ 2–3 mm; ≈ 0.2–0.3 mm at 10 atm). This is the length scale over which a single 'track' can fake a second, spatially separated cluster — the relevant figure of merit for two-track / delta-electron rejection.
- Because the mean is order unity, the illustrative PDG number is adequate for order-of-magnitude budgeting but should be replaced by a full Poisson/Rutherford sampling (Eq. 34.9 down to the detector's cluster threshold) if the budget needs better than ~30% on this term.
